Whenever the bluegrass musician Billy Strings has a couple of days off on the road, he’ll inevitably start rooting around for someplace to shop for watches. But unlike most stars of his magnitude Strings isn’t looking to sip champagne while perusing the latest luxury timepieces at a ritzy multi-level boutique. Instead, the 33-year-old feels far more at home in thrift shops and antique stores, where he can hunt for old pieces from the likes of Casio, Universal Genève, and Hamilton.
“That’s one of my favorite things to find: a tiny hole-in-the-wall store that has some cool vintage pieces,” Strings tells me over the phone.

The bluegrass star’s love of affordable throwback watches makes him a fitting frontman for the latest collaboration between Wind Vintage founder Eric Wind and True North Company. The Florida-based dealer has designed another spirited and colorful take on the upstart LA brand’s Vintage Rally Timer. The model is a loving homage to ’70s-era Rolex Daytonas—right down to its 37mm size, which Strings considers a plus for his smaller wrists.

This is the fourth release from Wind and TNC. It’s no surprise the pair keeps running it back: The three previous watches—inspired by everything from Wind’s love of playing Uno with his family to his daughter’s preference for pastels—all sold out immediately and often pop up on the secondary market for way above their $400 price tag. The new “Dreamsicle” edition makes good on its namesake with a soft orange dial and the collaboration’s now-signature multicolored subdials. (One apparent fan of the Easter-ish palette? Pope Leo XIV, who was given the watch by Wind on a recent trip to the Vatican.) The new piece—which is priced slightly higher than its predecessors at $490 and limited to 1,986 pieces—drops on October 2 at 1 p.m. EST via True North’s website.
I spoke with Billy Strings about starring in the collaboration’s accompanying campaign, his love of digging for secondhand watches, and the very special timepiece he wore when his son was born.

Billy Strings: I’m just a big fan of the niche vintage stuff. I got really into Accutrons—the old Spaceviews are the bluegrass watch. There was this guy named Tony Rice who collected them and worked on them. Tony Rice was the best bluegrass guitar player ever, so a lot of the bluegrass community is into these watches because it’s an if-you-know-you-know thing. I really got into those, old Ernest Borel cocktail watches, and some of these little vintage finds.

I like vintage stuff in general: old cars, old guitars. So when I started getting into watches, I immediately went toward the vintage stuff, and Eric is just one of the most knowledgeable cats in that world. He wanted to come to one of my concerts, and I was like, “Man, hell yeah, I’ll just put you on the guest list. While you’re at it, why don’t you bring me this Universal Genève Disco Volante watch?” which was on his site.

That’s another brand that I got really into, and that was before it came back. To me, it seemed like I found something that was my own, that not everybody was into. With Universal, you could find these really cool watches with an amazing design language, and these amazing vintage chronographs for a great price. So it was right up my alley: you could find a really cool-looking vintage watch, and you don’t have to spend an arm and a leg to get it.

He’s an amazing guy—he’s so smart, and he knows so much about these watches. So if I go find something on eBay, I can send it to him and say, “Hey, what’s up with this?” And he’ll say, “Oh, well, that’s not the correct crown,” or whatever.

He sent me the “Uno” one, and he asked me about this “Dreamsicle” thing and if I wanted to try it out. I love those watches because the design’s really smart. I love the proportions—it’s a smaller chronograph. A lot of modern watches just don’t fit me, I guess, because I have smaller wrists. And then just even taste-wise, I’m just not into some 45-millimeter crazy stuff.
I’ve always liked them because the Daytona inspiration is clear, but they’re doing their own distinct thing.

I love the playfulness of the color. They’re just really fun watches, and they’re quartz movements, so you just set it and forget it and it’s always on time. I’m not worried about banging it around or wearing the crap out of it. I’m super stoked on them, and I actually got my bandmates some.

There’s so much superficial stuff in this music industry, and I don’t want it to be about how I look, I want it to be about how I sound. So it’s whatever I’m feeling that specific day. I try to live in the moment as much as I can, from what I’m wearing to which song I’m playing to which watch I have on.
